deck.title: D550 Ethics for Accountants: Scenario Practice Exam
deck.description: 40 scenario questions from Mintz & Miller Ch. 3, 4, 8, weighted toward PA Attempt #1 misses (23 weak-spot items).
sources: Mintz & Miller, Ethical Obligations and Decision-Making in Accounting: Text and Cases (6th ed.; 2025 release slides), Ch. 3, 4, 8
Objective Assessment Notes (EthicsNotes.docx)
AICPA Code of Professional Conduct
SOX, Dodd-Frank, PSLRA, FCPA, Circular 230

questions.prompt:
The controller of a mid-size distributor is told her year-end bonus depends on hitting a revenue target. The company has one person who both records sales and approves credit memos. She books $400,000 of January shipments as December revenue and tells herself, "Everyone in this industry pulls sales forward, and it all evens out next quarter anyway."

Which element of the fraud triangle does the controller's statement to herself represent?

options.text: Situational pressure
Rationalization
Perceived opportunity
Scienter

questions.explanation: The fraud triangle has three elements: situational pressure (the bonus target), perceived opportunity (one person records sales and approves credit memos), and rationalization (the self-justifying story that "everyone does it" and "it evens out"). Her statement to herself is the rationalization. Scienter is a legal term for intent to deceive, not a fraud-triangle element.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-1: "Fraud in Organizations" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 17 ("Why Does Financial Statement Fraud Occur")
Notes, Ch. 3 ("fraud triangle")
PCAOB AS 2401, Consideration of Fraud in a Financial Statement Audit (fraud risk factors: incentives/pressures, opportunities, attitudes/rationalizations)

questions.prompt:
A CEO learns that several division heads have been pressuring the accounting staff to delay recording expenses so their divisions will hit targets tied to incentive pay. The CEO wants to discourage this behavior across the organization.

Which action would be most effective?

options.text: Eliminate all incentive compensation so no one has a reason to manipulate results
Remove division heads from the whistleblower reporting chain
Have the audit committee take over day-to-day management of the accounting department
Have senior management consistently communicate, and model, that ethics and integrity come before hitting the numbers

questions.explanation: The text calls support for ethical behavior from top management "a critical component of fostering an ethical climate." Poor tone at the top is the first factor listed as discouraging fraud reporting. Eliminating incentive pay (A) treats the symptom and ignores culture. Removing division heads from whistleblower channels (B) doesn't stop the pressure. The audit committee oversees financial reporting; it doesn't run the accounting department (C).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-3: "Ethics in the Workplace" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 24 ("Ethics in the Workplace"), slide 13 ("Poor tone at the top"), slide 51 ("Managers need to 'walk the talk'")
Notes, Ch. 3
COSO Internal Control: Integrated Framework (2013), Control Environment Principle 1: "The organization demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethical values."

questions.prompt:
A regional bank's employees routinely cut corners to meet aggressive sales quotas, and managers look the other way as long as targets are met. The new CEO wants to replace this "whatever-it-takes" mindset with an ethical climate.

Which step best supports that goal?

options.text: Tell employees to use their own professional judgment on ethical questions
Replace the internal audit department with an outside firm to monitor ethics compliance
Build ethical behavior into performance evaluations and reward employees whose conduct reflects the company's values
Publicly name employees who fail to meet sales quotas

questions.explanation: The last measure on Mintz's list for establishing an ethical culture is to "reward ethical behavior and include in performance evaluation system." A "whatever-it-takes" climate exists because the reward system values results over conduct, so changing what gets rewarded changes behavior. Leaving ethics to individual judgment (A) gives no structure. Outsourcing internal audit (B) isn't a culture fix; the text says to use internal auditors to investigate whether ethics policies are followed. Shaming low performers (D) increases pressure.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-3: "Ethics in the Workplace" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 24
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 20 ("Pressure to Maintain Numbers": "Financial results at all costs" is a sign of ethical collapse, per Marianne Jennings, The Seven Signs of Ethical Collapse, 2006)

questions.prompt:
The founders of an outdoor-gear company already run several CSR programs. They now want the company to formally adopt conscious capitalism as its approach to governance.

What should the founders do?

options.text: Anchor decisions in a higher purpose beyond profit and weigh the effects on all stakeholders, including employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and investors
Stop pursuing profit and redirect all earnings to environmental programs
Grant stock options to all employees so everyone has a financial stake
Focus exclusively on maximizing shareholder value, which will eventually benefit society

questions.explanation: Conscious capitalism has four guiding principles: higher purpose, stakeholder orientation, conscious leadership, and conscious culture. It "focuses on purpose beyond profit" but explicitly treats profit as "essential for a sustainable business." That's why B is wrong: it doesn't abandon profit. C is a compensation tactic, not a governance philosophy. D describes Friedman's economic model.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-5
Mintz Ch. 3, slides 38–39 (Whole Foods example: "Make their decisions based on stakeholder model")
Notes, Ch. 3 ("Conscious Capitalism: purpose beyond profit (decisions based on stakeholder model)")
John Mackey & Raj Sisodia, Conscious Capitalism (Harvard Business Review Press, 2013)

questions.prompt:
At a shareholder meeting, a CEO says: "Our one and only social responsibility is to use our resources to increase profits, as long as we play by the rules and don't engage in deception or fraud."

Which model of corporate social responsibility is the CEO describing?

options.text: Stakeholder model
Conscious capitalism
Economic model (managerial capitalism)
Triple bottom line

questions.explanation: The quote paraphrases Milton Friedman's view that business's "one and only social responsibility" is to increase profits within the rules of the game, without deception or fraud. Mintz calls this the dominant "managerial capitalism" model, which places shareholders at the center. The stakeholder model and conscious capitalism both extend responsibility to other groups. The triple bottom line reports on people, planet, and profit.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-5
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 40 ("Economic Model of CSR")
Milton Friedman, "The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits," New York Times Magazine, Sept. 13, 1970

questions.prompt:
A warehouse employee posts on Facebook that the company's new mandatory-overtime policy is unfair. Five coworkers reply, agree, and suggest they bring the issue to management together. The company fires the employee who wrote the original post.

Is the employee's post likely protected?

options.text: No, because the employee used a public website rather than an internal channel
Yes, because the post and replies amount to concerted activity about working conditions
Yes, but only if the employee belongs to a union
No, because the employee must first report the concern to Human Resources

questions.explanation: Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act protects employees' right to engage in "concerted activities for the purpose of … mutual aid or protection," whether or not they're unionized. When coworkers join the discussion about a shared working condition, the post becomes concerted activity. Union membership isn't required (C), and there's no rule requiring internal reporting first (D). In PA Q14 you chose "a single employee engaged in online activity," but the key fact is that others joined in or the post was made on behalf of the group.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-3: "Ethics in the Workplace" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 27 ("Using Social Media to Criticize the Employer")
Notes, Ch. 3 ("Others commenting on workplace post = concerted effort")
Hispanics United of Buffalo, Inc., 359 NLRB No. 37 (2012) (Facebook posts responded to by coworkers were protected concerted activity)
NLRB, "Concerted Activity," nlrb.gov

questions.prompt:
An accounts-payable clerk, frustrated after a bad performance review, posts on social media that her supervisor is "clueless." No coworkers comment or engage, and the post doesn't mention wages, hours, or any group concern. She is disciplined.

How would the NLRB most likely view the post?

options.text: Protected, because all employee speech about an employer is protected
Protected, because it was posted outside working hours
Not protected, because it is an individual "personal gripe" rather than concerted activity
Not protected, because social-media speech is never covered by the NLRA

questions.explanation: This is the flip side of the concerted-activity rule. When a comment is made solely by the individual with no input from others, the NLRB treats it as a "personal gripe," which isn't protected. A is too broad. B is irrelevant, because off-duty timing doesn't create protection. D is wrong because social-media posts can be protected when concerted.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-3: "Ethics in the Workplace" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 27

questions.prompt:
A CFO reviews the company's 10-K, knows the financial statements contain a material departure from GAAP, and still willfully signs the written statement certifying that the report fully complies with SEC reporting requirements.

Which Sarbanes-Oxley section carries the criminal penalties for this conduct?

options.text: Section 906
Section 806
Section 404
Section 103

questions.explanation: Section 906 requires a written statement by the CEO and CFO that each periodic report fully complies with the Exchange Act and fairly presents the company's financial condition. It adds criminal penalties: knowingly certifying a noncompliant report carries up to $1 million and 10 years in prison, and willfully certifying carries up to $5 million and 20 years. The word "willfully" in the question points to 906. Section 806 is whistleblower anti-retaliation, 404 is internal-control reporting, and 103 is PCAOB auditing standards. (PA Q10 had this exact concept, and you chose 103.)
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 45
Notes, Ch. 3 ("906 – statement by CEO/CFO about compliance with SEC reporting requirements")
Sarbanes-Oxley Act §906, codified at 18 U.S.C. §1350(c)

questions.prompt:
Each quarter, a CEO and CFO sign a certification that they reviewed the 10-Q, that it contains no untrue statement of material fact, that they are responsible for disclosure controls, and that they have disclosed all significant control deficiencies to the auditors and the audit committee.

Which SOX section requires this certification?

options.text: Section 301
Section 404
Section 406
Section 302

questions.explanation: Section 302 is the civil certification in each 10-Q and 10-K. It covers no untrue statements or omissions, responsibility for disclosure controls, and disclosure of significant deficiencies and fraud to auditors and the audit committee. Memory hook: 302 is the certification language inside the report, and 906 is the separate criminal certification attached to it. Section 301 covers the audit committee, 404 covers internal-control reports, and 406 covers the code of ethics for senior financial officers.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 44
Mintz Ch. 8, slide 55
SEC Rules 13a-14 and 15d-14

questions.prompt:
A listed company's board wants to add a retired partner of the company's outside law firm to the audit committee. The law firm still receives about $250,000 a year in legal-advisory fees from the company, and the retiree receives a share of those fees.

Under SOX Section 301 and SEC Rule 10A-3, what is the problem?

options.text: Audit committee members must be licensed CPAs
Audit committee members may not accept, directly or indirectly, any consulting, advisory, or other compensatory fee from the company
Audit committees must have between five and eight members
At least one audit committee member must be a major shareholder

questions.explanation: Rule 10A-3(b)(1), implementing SOX §301, requires every audit committee member to be independent. A member may not "accept directly or indirectly any consulting, advisory, or other compensatory fee" from the issuer (other than board fees) and may not be an affiliated person. Indirect fees through a law firm the member shares in count. There's no CPA requirement (A); SOX §407 only requires disclosure of whether at least one member is a "financial expert." There's no size rule (C) and no shareholding requirement (D).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Mintz Ch. 3, slides 44 and 48

questions.prompt:
An audit senior at a CPA firm concludes that her firm failed to follow the illegal-acts procedures required by Section 10A of the Securities Exchange Act after discovering a client's likely fraud. She raised the issue with firm leadership, who refused to act. She is worried that going outside the firm will violate client confidentiality.

What recourse does Dodd-Frank give her?

options.text: None; the confidentiality rule prohibits any disclosure outside the firm
Resign, because resigning ends all of her disclosure obligations
Make a whistleblower submission to the SEC alleging that her own firm failed to comply with Section 10A or professional standards
Post the details publicly so investors are warned

questions.explanation:
Under SEC whistleblower rules, an auditor or employee of the audit firm may make a submission "alleging that the firm failed to assess, investigate or report wrongdoing in accordance with Section 10A, or that the firm failed to follow other professional standards." Whistleblowing in conformity with Dodd-Frank "sets aside the confidentiality requirement," so A is wrong. Resigning doesn't "negate the auditor's disclosure responsibilities to the SEC," so B is wrong. Public posting (D) isn't a protected channel. (In PA Q18 you chose "report the financial wrongdoing directly to the SEC." The tested concept is that her claim is against her own firm for failing to act.)
Section 10A process to know: The auditor reports to the board. The board has 1 business day to notify the SEC and give the auditor a copy. If the auditor doesn't receive the copy, it must furnish its own report to the SEC within 1 business day (or resign and furnish the report).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-7: "Whistleblowing" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slides 63, 65, 66, 67
Notes, Ch. 3 ("Dodd Frank: sets aside confidentiality requirement … resignation from the audit firm does not negate the auditor's disclosure responsibilities")
Dodd-Frank §922, adding Exchange Act §21F, 15 U.S.C. §78u-6
SEC Rule 21F-4(b)(4)
Exchange Act §10A(b), 15 U.S.C. §78j-1(b)
ET 1.700.001 (disclosure permitted to comply with laws and regulations)

questions.prompt:
An internal auditor at a public company reports suspected revenue manipulation to the chief audit executive and the audit committee. After 130 days, no investigation has begun and nothing has changed. The internal auditor then reports the matter to the SEC.

Is the internal auditor eligible for a Dodd-Frank whistleblower award?

options.text: Yes, because she first reported internally and at least 120 days passed without action
No, because internal auditors are permanently excluded from awards
No, because the report went to the audit committee instead of the SEC first
Yes, but only if she resigns before submitting the tip

questions.explanation: Internal auditors and compliance personnel are usually excluded from awards because of their pre-existing duty to report. They become eligible if (1) disclosure is needed to prevent substantial injury to the entity or investors, (2) they reasonably believe the entity is impeding an investigation, or (3) they reported internally and at least 120 days passed with no action. Awards are 10–30% of sanctions over $1 million.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-7: "Whistleblowing" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slides 63–64
Notes, Ch. 3
SEC Rule 21F-4(b)(4)(iii) and (v), 17 C.F.R. §240.21F-4

questions.prompt:
A controller reports possible securities-law violations only to the company's general counsel and CFO. He never contacts the SEC. Two weeks later, he is fired, and he sues under Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision.

Based on Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers, what is the likely outcome?

options.text: He wins, because internal reporting is fully protected under Dodd-Frank
He wins, because confidentiality agreements cannot block whistleblower rights
He loses under every federal statute, because he never went public
He is not protected under Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision, because he did not report to the SEC (though he may have a SOX §806 claim)

questions.explanation: In Digital Realty, the Supreme Court held unanimously that Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision protects only people who have reported to the SEC. An employee who reported only internally may still sue under SOX §806, which covers internal reports to a supervisor, but that route has a shorter filing deadline and different remedies. B states the holding of Erhart v. BofI, which is true but doesn't answer this question.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-7: "Whistleblowing" section
Mintz Ch. 3, slides 69–70
Notes, Ch. 3 ("Whistleblowers not protected against retaliation under Dodd-Frank unless they first report to SEC")
Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers, 583 U.S. 149 (2018)

questions.prompt:
A sole practitioner CPA has not filed his personal federal income tax returns for three years, even though he owed tax each year. None of his clients are affected.

Which AICPA rule has the CPA most directly violated?

options.text: Integrity and Objectivity Rule
General Standards Rule
Compliance With Standards Rule
Acts Discreditable Rule

questions.explanation: Failure to file a tax return or pay a tax liability is specifically listed as an act discreditable under the Code, because it brings discredit on the profession even when no client is involved. The other options apply to professional services performed for clients.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-6: "Rules for the Performance of Professional Services" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 37 ("Failure of a CPA/CPA firm to file and pay taxes")
Notes, Ch. 4 ("Acts Discreditable … failure of CPA to pay taxes")
ET 1.400.001 (Acts Discreditable Rule) and ET 1.400.030 (Failure to File a Tax Return or Pay a Tax Liability)

questions.prompt: Which scenario is a violation of the Acts Discreditable Rule?

options.text: A firm staffs a school-district audit with a CPA who has no governmental audit experience
A CPA prepares the financial statements of a private company that is also the firm's audit client
A newly licensed CPA posts the questions she remembers from her CPA exam section in an online study group
A CPA signs off on financial statements containing a material departure from GAAP

questions.explanation:
Soliciting or disclosing CPA exam questions and answers is an enumerated act discreditable. To sort the distractors, match each to the rule it tests:
- A is a competence issue under the General Standards Rule (ET 1.300.001).
- B is a nonattest-service/independence issue (ET 1.295).
- D falls under the Accounting Principles Rule (ET 1.320.001). Negligence in preparing financial statements is also an act discreditable (ET 1.400.040), but C is the cleanest, textbook-listed example.

Other listed acts discreditable include discrimination and harassment (ET 1.400.010), failure to file or pay taxes (ET 1.400.030), and not following governmental audit requirements (ET 1.400.050).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-6: "Rules for the Performance of Professional Services" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slides 37–38 (Big Four internal-exam cheating was an "act discreditable")
Notes, Ch. 4
ET 1.400.020 (Solicitation or Disclosure of CPA Examination Questions and Answers)

questions.prompt:
A client for whom a CPA prepares tax returns only (no attest services) sends the CPA an expensive bottle of wine after the CPA finishes the returns early. The CPA's firm has no written policy on gifts.

What should the CPA do under the AICPA Code?

options.text: Evaluate whether accepting the gift is reasonable in the circumstances, meaning a reasonable and informed third party wouldn't conclude the CPA's objectivity is compromised
Accept it automatically, because the firm has no policy prohibiting gifts
Ask the client to give the gift to the firm instead of the individual CPA
Ask the client to wait until next tax season to give the gift

questions.explanation: For clients where independence isn't at issue, the Code's gifts-and-entertainment interpretation says threats to objectivity (self-interest, familiarity, undue influence) are at an acceptable level if the gift is reasonable in the circumstances. The CPA weighs the nature, value, frequency, and timing of the gift. "Acceptable level" means a reasonable and informed third party wouldn't conclude compliance is compromised. The absence of a firm policy doesn't end the analysis (B), and redirecting the gift to the firm (C) or delaying it (D) doesn't remove the threat. (On PA Q3 you chose C.)
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
ET 1.120.010 (Offering or Accepting Gifts or Entertainment, under the Integrity and Objectivity Rule)
ET 0.400 (definition of "acceptable level")
ET 1.000.010 (conceptual framework)
Mintz Ch. 4, slides 10 and 29

questions.prompt:
During fieldwork, the CFO of an audit client gives the in-charge audit senior a $600 designer watch "as thanks for the smooth audit."

What is the correct response under the AICPA independence rules?

options.text: Accept it, because gifts after fieldwork has started don't affect independence
Accept it but disclose it in the audit report
Decline it, because accepting a gift from an attest client impairs independence unless its value is clearly insignificant to the recipient
Accept it if the engagement partner approves

questions.explanation: Under the Independence Rule, accepting a gift from an attest client impairs independence unless the value is clearly insignificant to the recipient. That's a stricter test than for nonattest clients. Entertainment from an attest client is judged on whether it's reasonable in the circumstances. A $600 watch isn't clearly insignificant. Disclosure (B) and partner approval (D) don't cure the impairment.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
ET 1.285.010 (Gifts and Entertainment, under the Independence Rule)
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 13 (financial self-interest threat)

questions.prompt:
A CPA firm provides monthly bookkeeping, payroll processing, and income-tax preparation to a small business. The firm performs no audit, review, compilation, or other attest work for this client. A competitor claims the firm is violating the Independence Rule.

Is the competitor correct?

options.text: Yes, because providing bookkeeping creates a self-review threat
No, because the Independence Rule applies only when the firm performs attest engagements
Yes, because providing more than one service creates a familiarity threat
No, because different staff members perform each service

questions.explanation: The Independence Rule requires independence "in the performance of professional services as required by standards promulgated by bodies designated by Council," which means audits, reviews, examinations, and other attest engagements. Bookkeeping, payroll, and tax work for a non-attest client don't require independence. Options A and C name real threats, but those threats matter only when there is an attest engagement to protect. D is irrelevant. (PA Q4 had this concept. The PA's keyed answer was worded oddly, but the underlying rule is that no attest engagement means no Independence Rule violation.)
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
ET 1.200.001 (Independence Rule)
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 10 ("Independence for Members in Public Practice")
Notes, Ch. 4 ("Independence required for audit and attestation services")

questions.prompt:
A CPA firm audits a privately held manufacturer and also wants to post its monthly journal entries. The firm wants to stay independent.

Which condition must be met?

options.text: The firm must assign different staff to the bookkeeping and the audit, and that alone is sufficient
The client's audit committee must preapprove the service, as required by SOX
The firm must disclose the bookkeeping service in its audit opinion

The client must agree to assume all management responsibilities and designate an individual with suitable skill, knowledge, and/or experience to oversee the service, evaluate its adequacy, and accept responsibility for the results

questions.explanation: A CPA may perform some nonattest services, including bookkeeping, for a private attest client without impairing independence, as long as the member doesn't assume management responsibilities. The client must agree to (1) assume all management responsibilities, (2) oversee the service through an individual with suitable skill, knowledge, and/or experience, (3) evaluate the adequacy and results, and (4) accept responsibility for the results. Separate staffing alone isn't enough (A). Audit-committee preapproval (B) is a SOX/PCAOB requirement for public companies. Disclosure in the opinion (C) isn't a cure.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 19 ("Providing Nonattest Services to an Attest Client")
ET 1.295.040 (General Requirements for Performing Nonattest Services)
ET 1.295.120 (Bookkeeping, Payroll, and Disbursement)

questions.prompt:
A CPA firm designed and implemented a financial information system for Company B. Company B is then acquired and becomes an affiliate of Company A, one of the firm's audit clients. The firm concludes that the system work is "immaterial" to Company A's consolidated statements and continues both engagements.

What is the concern with the firm's reasoning?

options.text: Using materiality to dismiss a nonaudit service that would be prohibited at the audit client itself creates a threat to independence
The firm has committed fraud by continuing both engagements
The firm has violated the Accounting Principles Rule
The firm has taken on an advocacy role for Company A

questions.explanation: Mintz specifically criticizes firms that use a materiality criterion to decide whether nonaudit services to an affiliate, which would be prohibited if provided to the parent, violate independence. "Applying such a materiality standard can have the effect of dismissing otherwise improper relationships." The firm designed a financial information system, which is a SOX-prohibited service for issuer audit clients, and then audits results the system produces. That's a self-review threat to independence. The facts involve no fraud (B), no GAAP departure (C), and no promotion of the client (D). (On PA Q6 you chose "compromising the accounting principles.")
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-3: "SEC Actions on Auditor Independence" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slides 27–28 ("Materiality Issues")
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 15 (SOX nonaudit services)
ET 1.224.010 (Client Affiliates)

questions.prompt:
After a dispute over last year's audit, an audit client files a lawsuit alleging that the CPA firm's negligence caused the client's losses. The firm is scheduled to begin this year's audit next month.

Which threat to independence is most significant?

options.text: Familiarity
Undue influence
Adverse interest
Management participation

questions.explanation: Adverse interest is "commencing, or the expressed intention to commence, litigation by either the client or the CPA against the other." When the parties are legal adversaries, the auditor can't be objective. Undue influence (B) would be a threat to replace the firm over an accounting disagreement.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 13 (Exhibit 4.1)
Notes, Ch. 4 ("adverse interest: commencing litigation against one another")
ET 1.000.010 (conceptual framework threats)
ET 1.290.010 (Actual or Threatened Litigation)

questions.prompt:
Because an audit client's accounting clerk quit, the audit staff prepare the client's sales journal and source documents. Those documents are then used to generate the financial statements that the same firm audits.

Which threat to independence does this create?

options.text: Advocacy
Self-review
Adverse interest
Financial self-interest

questions.explanation: Mintz's example of self-review is "preparing source documents used to generate the client's financial statements." The firm would be auditing its own work, which also violates the SEC principle that an auditor cannot audit its own work. Preparing source documents can also shade into a management-participation threat, but self-review is the textbook classification.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-2: "AICPA Code: Independence Considerations for Members in Public Practice" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 13 (Exhibit 4.1)
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 21 (three SEC principles)
SEC Regulation S-X Rule 2-01, 17 C.F.R. §210.2-01 (preliminary note)

questions.prompt:
A CPA is hired to prepare a client's current-year return and discovers that the client's prior-year return (prepared by someone else) understated taxable income by $18,000.

What is the CPA's responsibility under Treasury Circular 230 and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services (SSTS)?

options.text: File an amended return for the client immediately
Notify the IRS of the error in writing
Wait to see whether the IRS detects the error
Promptly inform the client of the error and its possible consequences, and recommend corrective measures

questions.explanation: Under Circular 230 §10.21, a practitioner who learns of a client's error or omission must promptly advise the client of it and of the consequences. The revised SSTS (effective January 1, 2024) similarly require the member to inform the taxpayer promptly and recommend corrective measures. The decision to amend belongs to the taxpayer. The CPA doesn't file an amended return on their own (A) and doesn't notify the IRS (B). Waiting (C) ignores the duty. (On PA Q7 you chose "report the error to the IRS.")
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-7: "Ethics and Tax Services" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 50 ("Treasury Circular 230: Knowledge of error return. Advise client … Taxpayer decides whether to correct the error")
Notes, Ch. 4 ("Treasury Circular 230 – knowledge of error = advise client and they decide what to do")
AICPA SSTS No. 1, §1.2 (Knowledge of Errors)

questions.prompt:
A CPA preparing a client's current-year return found an $18,000 understatement of income on the client's prior-year return and advised the client of the error. The client refuses to amend the prior-year return.

What should the CPA do next?

options.text: Consider whether to withdraw from the engagement, and not disclose the error to the IRS without the client's consent
Report the error to the IRS, because confidentiality does not apply to tax matters
File the amended return without the client's permission
Continue as usual; the CPA has no further obligation of any kind

questions.explanation: If the client won't correct the error, the SSTS say the member should consider whether to withdraw from the engagement and whether to continue the professional relationship. The member is still bound by confidentiality and may not inform the taxing authority without the client's consent, unless required by law. If the member keeps preparing returns, they should take reasonable steps so the error isn't repeated. B and C violate the Confidential Client Information Rule. D ignores the duty to reconsider the relationship.

questions.prompt: Which fee arrangement is permitted under the AICPA Contingent Fees Rule?

options.text: A fee equal to 20% of the refund on an original income-tax return prepared for a nonattest client
A consulting fee contingent on cost savings, charged to a company whose financial statements the firm audits
A contingent fee for representing a client in an IRS-initiated examination, where the fee depends on the findings of the IRS
A contingent fee for a compilation that the client will give to its bank, where the report doesn't disclose a lack of independence

questions.explanation: Contingent fees are prohibited for any client for whom the firm performs an audit, review, certain compilations, or an examination of prospective financial information (B and D). They're also prohibited for preparing an original or amended tax return or refund claim, for any client (A). The Code permits fees based on the results of judicial proceedings or the findings of governmental agencies, such as representing a client in an IRS-initiated examination.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-6: "Rules for the Performance of Professional Services" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 39

questions.prompt:
A CPA receives a validly issued, enforceable subpoena from a state court ordering production of a client's working papers in a civil case. The client hasn't consented to the disclosure.

What should the CPA do?

options.text: Refuse, because disclosing client information always requires client consent
Comply, because responding to a valid subpoena is a recognized exception to the Confidential Client Information Rule
Comply only after resigning from the engagement
Refuse unless the Board of Accountancy approves in writing

questions.explanation: The Confidential Client Information Rule generally requires client consent, but it expressly doesn't prevent a member from complying with a validly issued and enforceable subpoena or summons. Other exceptions include complying with laws and regulations (such as Dodd-Frank), peer review, and responding to or initiating an ethics investigation.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-6: "Rules for the Performance of Professional Services" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 41 ("Confidentiality")

questions.prompt:
A CPA working as assistant controller at a private company believes the CFO is directing a material revenue-recognition treatment that misstates the financial statements. The CFO dismisses her concerns.

According to the AICPA guidance on subordination of judgment for members in business, what should she do first after the CFO rejects her position?

options.text: Resign immediately without documenting anything
Go directly to the press to protect investors
Record the entry as directed, since the CFO has final authority
Take the matter to a higher level of management or to those charged with governance (such as the audit committee), document her concerns, and consider consulting legal counsel

questions.explanation: The Integrity and Objectivity Rule prohibits knowingly misrepresenting facts or subordinating one's judgment. For members in business, the interpretation lays out the path. First, discuss with the supervisor. If that doesn't resolve it and the misstatement is material, take the matter to appropriate higher management or those charged with governance, such as the audit committee. Document the understanding of the facts, the standards involved, and the parties consulted. Then consider consulting legal counsel, whether to continue the relationship, and any obligation to communicate with third parties. Resigning with no documentation (A) skips steps. Going to the press (B) violates confidentiality. Complying (C) is subordination of judgment.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-4: "AICPA Code: Ethical Conflicts" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 32 ("Subordination of Judgment")
Mintz Ch. 3, slide 66 ("Integrity Considerations")
ET 2.130.020 (Subordination of Judgment, members in business)
ET 1.130.020 (the equivalent for members in public practice)

questions.prompt:
An audit firm registered with the PCAOB wants to prepare personal income-tax returns for the CFO of an issuer audit client. The CFO has held the position throughout the audit period.

Under PCAOB Rule 3523, what is the result?

options.text: Independence is impaired, because the firm would provide tax services to a person in a financial reporting oversight role at an audit client
Independence isn't affected, because personal returns aren't related to the audit
It's permitted if the audit committee preapproves under Rule 3524
It's permitted if the fees are immaterial to the firm

questions.explanation: A registered firm isn't independent if it provides tax services to a person in a financial reporting oversight role (FROR) at an issuer audit client during the audit and professional engagement period. The narrow exceptions cover a person who serves only as a board member, a person in a FROR only at an affiliate whose financial statements are immaterial, or a person who wasn't in the role when the engagement began. A CFO in the role throughout fits none of these. Audit-committee preapproval (C, Rule 3524) can't cure a prohibited service.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 4 (begins p. 174), LO 4-8: "PCAOB Rules" section
Mintz Ch. 4, slide 54 ("PCAOB Rules")

PCAOB Rule 3523, Tax Services for Persons in Financial Reporting Oversight Roles

questions.prompt:
An auditor fails to detect that a client's warehouse manager has been stealing inventory for two years. The client ignored the auditor's written recommendations to separate custody and recordkeeping duties. The client sues the auditor for audit malpractice.

Which defense best fits the facts?

options.text: Lack of privity between the auditor and the client
Section 11 due diligence defense
Comparative negligence, apportioning fault between the client and the auditor
The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act's safe harbor for forward-looking statements

questions.explanation: Courts now allow accountants to assert a comparative negligence defense, which allocates fault and damages between the accountant and the client. The client ignored the auditor's written segregation-of-duties recommendations, so its own negligence contributed to the loss. Privity (A) exists with the client, so it's no defense. Section 11 (B) applies to registration statements. The PSLRA safe harbor (D) covers forward-looking statements. Note: in PA Q23 you chose the "audit-interference rule." That rule actually limits a client-negligence defense to cases where the client's negligence interfered with the audit, so it isn't a way to shift all fault to the client. Contributory negligence is the older all-or-nothing defense that comparative negligence largely replaced.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 11–12 ("Defending Audit-Malpractice Cases"; "Comparative Negligence")
Notes, Ch. 8 ("Comparative negligence – formula based on allocation of fault between accountant and client")

questions.prompt:
A lender that was never named in the engagement letter and never communicated with the auditor lends money to a client based on its audited statements. The lender sues the auditor for ordinary negligence in a state that follows Ultramares v. Touche.

What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The lender recovers, because all users of financial statements are owed a duty of care
The lender can't recover for ordinary negligence without privity, although claims for gross negligence or fraud remain open
The lender recovers, because the auditor should have foreseen the loan
The lender can't recover under any theory, including fraud

questions.explanation: In Ultramares, Judge Cardozo held that a third party not in privity can't recover from an auditor for ordinary negligence, because auditors would otherwise face "liability in an indeterminate amount for an indeterminate time to an indeterminate class." The court left the door open for gross negligence and fraud, which is why D is wrong.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slide 8
Notes, Ch. 8 ("A third party not in privity can not sue for negligence – left door open for gross negligence and fraud")
Ultramares Corp. v. Touche, 255 N.Y. 170 (1931). (The slide lists the year as 1933, but the decision was issued in 1931.)

questions.prompt:
Before starting an audit, an auditor learns that a specific bank will use the audited statements to decide on a $5 million line of credit. The auditor meets with the bank's loan officer and sends the signed audit report directly to the bank.

Under Credit Alliance and Security Pacific, how would these facts be characterized?

options.text: No relationship, because the bank didn't pay the audit fee
A "grapevine" relationship
Reasonably foreseeable reliance only
A near-privity relationship, so the auditor can be liable to the bank for negligence

questions.explanation: Credit Alliance set a three-part test: (1) the auditor knew the statements would be used for a particular purpose, (2) a known party intended to rely on them, and (3) some conduct by the auditor links it to that party. Security Pacific sharpened the third prong: the auditor must directly convey the report to the third party or act to induce its reliance. Meeting with the loan officer and sending the report directly satisfies all three. "Grapevine" plaintiffs (B), from Murphy v. BDO Seidman, rely indirectly on what others told them.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 16 and 20
Notes, Ch. 8 ("Near-privity")
Credit Alliance Corp. v. Arthur Andersen & Co., 65 N.Y.2d 536 (1985)
Security Pacific Business Credit, Inc. v. Peat Marwick Main & Co., 79 N.Y.2d 695 (1992)

questions.prompt:
In a state that follows H. Rosenblum, Inc. v. Adler, an investor who bought a company's stock based on its audited statements sues the auditor for negligence. The auditor didn't know this investor existed.

What standard applies?

options.text: The auditor owes a duty of care to all reasonably foreseeable third parties who receive and rely on the statements for proper business purposes
The auditor is liable only to parties in contractual privity
The auditor is liable only to a known person relying for a known purpose
The auditor is liable only if it acted with scienter

questions.explanation: Rosenblum is the broadest approach. Auditors owe a duty "to all persons whom the auditor should reasonably foresee as recipients of the statements from the company for proper business purposes, provided the recipients rely on those statements." B is Ultramares, C is the strict "known person, known purpose" standard (McCamish), and D is the fraud standard. California rejected Rosenblum in Bily v. Arthur Young (1992).
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 19–20
Notes, Ch. 8 ("Auditors can be liable to all reasonably foreseeable third parties")
H. Rosenblum, Inc. v. Adler, 93 N.J. 324 (1983)
Bily v. Arthur Young & Co., 3 Cal. 4th 370 (1992)

questions.prompt:
A first-year audit associate isn't aware that the auditing standards require confirming certain receivables. He doesn't send confirmations, and a material overstatement goes undetected. He had no intent to deceive and didn't realize the risk he was taking, though a competent auditor would have.

Which liability theory best describes his conduct?

options.text: Fraud
Recklessness
Negligence
Constructive fraud

questions.explanation: Negligence is failing to take reasonable care, where the person is not aware of the risk but should have been. Recklessness means the person is aware of the risk and consciously disregards it. Fraud requires scienter, meaning intent to deceive. Constructive fraud (gross negligence) is carelessness so extreme it implies reckless disregard for due care. The associate didn't know the standard and had no intent, which fits ordinary negligence.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 13 and 15 (Exhibit 8.3, "Negligence vs. Recklessness") and slide 21
Notes, Ch. 8 ("negligence: unknowingly taking a risk; recklessness: knowingly taking a risk")

questions.prompt:
Investors sue an audit firm under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, alleging that the audit opinion was false.

Beyond showing a material misstatement, reliance, loss, and causation, what must the plaintiffs specifically plead and prove?

options.text: That the auditor failed to follow GAAS
Scienter, meaning intent to deceive, manipulate, or defraud, pled with facts giving rise to a strong inference
That the auditor breached its duty of care through ordinary negligence
That the auditor was in privity of contract with each investor

questions.explanation: For a Rule 10b-5 claim, the plaintiff must prove a material misrepresentation or omission, scienter, a connection to a purchase or sale, reliance, economic loss, and loss causation. Ordinary negligence isn't enough (Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder). Under the PSLRA, scienter must be pled with particularized facts giving rise to a strong inference (Tellabs). This connects to PA Q20, which you answered correctly ("intent to deceive"). GAAS noncompliance (A) and breach of duty of care (C) are negligence concepts.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 23 and 46
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 51–52 (PSLRA; Tellabs)
Ernst & Ernst v. Hochfelder, 425 U.S. 185 (1976)
Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308 (2007)

questions.prompt:
A bankruptcy trustee sues an audit firm, claiming its negligent audits let a dot-com company keep operating and lose hundreds of millions. The firm shows that the losses came from the collapse of the internet market, which destroyed the value of all similar companies.

Based on Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, which defense is available?

options.text: The losses weren't caused by the audit; they resulted from market-wide conditions (loss causation)
The auditor's misstatements directly caused the losses
The firm intentionally deceived the investors
The firm violated the PSLRA

questions.explanation: In Maxwell, the Seventh Circuit (Judge Posner) affirmed judgment for KPMG. The dot-com company's losses were caused by the collapse of the internet market, not by the audits, so the trustee couldn't show the audit caused the harm. Mintz summarizes: "Maxwell's harm wasn't caused by KPMG's audit." B is the plaintiff's argument, and C and D are not defenses. (On PA Q26 you chose B.)
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slide 46 ("Section 10 and Rule 10b-5")
Maxwell v. KPMG LLP, 520 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2008)

Cleary Gottlieb, "Maxwell v. KPMG LLP: Seventh Circuit Applies Principle of 'Loss Causation'" (2008). For the related federal securities-law principle, see Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Broudo, 544 U.S. 336 (2005)

questions.prompt: Which law expanded the scope of third parties to whom auditors owe a duty of care? (For example, it requires the auditor to attest to management's internal-control report, which exposes auditors to liability for undisclosed material weaknesses.)

options.text: The Dodd-Frank Act
The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX)

questions.explanation: Mintz states: "SOX increases auditor liability to third parties by specifying or expanding the scope of third parties to whom an auditor owes a duty of care." Section 404 requires the auditor to attest to management's internal-control assessment, and failing to disclose detected material weaknesses exposes the auditor to Section 11 liability. The PSLRA (B) narrowed exposure through proportionate liability. Dodd-Frank (A) is about whistleblowers. (On PA Q27 you chose Dodd-Frank.)
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-5: "SOX and Auditor Legal Liabilities" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slide 54
Notes, Ch. 8 ("SOX Section 404 – expands liability of auditor duty of care")

questions.prompt:
A large public company and its much smaller audit firm are both sued for securities fraud. The jury finds the company knowingly committed fraud, but the audit firm acted without knowledge. The jury assigns the audit firm 10% of the fault.

How does the PSLRA affect the audit firm?

options.text: It's jointly and severally liable for 100% of the damages
It can't settle unless the corporation settles
It's generally liable only for its proportionate share of the damages
It's automatically dismissed because it lacked intent

questions.explanation: The PSLRA replaced joint and several liability with proportionate liability for defendants who didn't knowingly commit the violation. The firm pays generally its share, here 10%. Two exceptions to know: (1) if another defendant's share is uncollectible, proportionately liable defendants can be charged up to an extra 50% of their own share, and (2) certain small investors can still collect jointly and severally. A describes the pre-PSLRA rule. (On PA Q29 you chose "joint and several.")
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slide 52 ("Proportionate Liability – PSLRA")
Notes, Ch. 8 ("Proportionate liability for non-knowing securities violations")
Exchange Act §21D(f), 15 U.S.C. §78u-4(f)

questions.prompt: Under the PSLRA, when is a defendant in a private securities action subject to joint and several liability?

options.text: Whenever the defendant is an auditor
When the trier of fact finds the defendant knowingly committed a violation of the securities laws
Whenever total damages exceed $1 million
Never, because the PSLRA eliminated joint and several liability

questions.explanation: Only defendants found to have knowingly committed a securities violation remain jointly and severally liable. Knowing violators can be made to pay the full judgment. This is the mirror image of the proportionate-liability rule.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slide 52 ("Only those who committed 'knowing' securities fraud will suffer joint and several liability")

questions.prompt:
An audit firm is sued under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933 because the audited financial statements in a registration statement contained a material misstatement.

To establish a due diligence defense, what must the auditor show?

options.text: After a reasonable investigation, it had reasonable ground to believe, and did believe, that its expertised statements were true and not misleading
The plaintiff didn't read the registration statement
The misstatement was later corrected in a 10-Q
The auditor wasn't in privity with the plaintiff

questions.explanation: Section 11 imposes liability for material misstatements or omissions in a registration statement. Plaintiffs don't need to prove reliance or scienter, so B is wrong. An expert such as the auditor has a due diligence defense for its expertised portion. It must show that, after reasonable investigation, it had reasonable ground to believe, and did believe, the statements were true with no material omission. Privity (D) is irrelevant under Section 11. You answered this correctly on PA Q24.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 38–43 (Securities Act of 1933; Section 11; Omnicare)
Securities Act §11(b)(3)(B), 15 U.S.C. §77k(b)(3)
Omnicare, Inc. v. Laborers Dist. Council Constr. Indus. Pension Fund, 575 U.S. 175 (2015)
Escott v. BarChris Construction Corp., 283 F. Supp. 643 (S.D.N.Y. 1968)

questions.prompt:
A U.S. manufacturer's local agent pays a customs clerk in a foreign country a small fee to process, on time, the paperwork for a shipment that already qualifies for release. The clerk has no discretion over whether the goods clear.

How is this payment most likely treated under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act?

options.text: A prohibited bribe, because any payment to a foreign official violates the FCPA
Legal only if the payment is recorded as a bribe in the books
Protected by the "local law" affirmative defense
A facilitating (grease) payment for routine governmental action, which the FCPA's anti-bribery provisions exempt

questions.explanation:
A facilitating fee is "a payment made to speed up … a task that is within a person's normal range of authorized activities," such as routine governmental action like processing papers. A bribe is paid to change behavior or obtain something outside the official's authorized duties. The FCPA excepts facilitating payments for routine governmental action.
- The Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988 amended the FCPA to add the two affirmative defenses and to clarify the knowledge standard (PA Q25).
- The two affirmative defenses are (1) the payment was lawful under the foreign country's written laws, and (2) it was a reasonable and bona fide expenditure, such as travel and lodging, directly related to promoting or demonstrating products or performing a contract (PA Q28).

The "local law" defense (C) requires written local law permitting the payment, which isn't present here.
Penalty note: the slides list $1M for corporations and $10,000 for individuals. The current statute provides up to $2M per anti-bribery violation for entities and up to $100,000 plus 5 years in prison for individuals, with higher fines possible under the Alternative Fines Act. Employers may not pay an individual's fine. Know the textbook figures for the OA, but be aware the law has changed.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-6: "Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)" section
Mintz Ch. 8, slides 57–58
Notes, Ch. 8 ("bribe … facilitation fee")
15 U.S.C. §78dd-1(b) (exception) and §78dd-1(c) (affirmative defenses)
15 U.S.C. §78dd-2(g) (penalties)

questions.prompt:
Dana Ruiz, CFO of Halvorsen Freight (a public company), knows the third-quarter 10-Q overstates revenue by $4.2 million through fictitious shipments. She signs the written statement accompanying the report, swearing it fully complies with the Exchange Act and fairly presents the company's financial condition. She does it deliberately to protect the stock price before her options vest.

Which Sarbanes-Oxley section's criminal penalties apply most directly to her willful false statement?

options.text: Section 906
Section 806
Section 103
Section 301

questions.explanation: Section 906 requires the CEO and CFO to furnish a written statement that each periodic report complies with the Exchange Act and fairly presents the company's financial condition, and it attaches criminal penalties: up to $1 million and 10 years for knowingly certifying a noncompliant report, and up to $5 million and 20 years for doing it willfully. Section 806 protects whistleblowers from retaliation, Section 103 directs the PCAOB to set auditing, quality-control and independence standards, and Section 301 covers audit committee independence. On PA Q10 you chose Section 103; the word "willfully" plus a CEO/CFO statement points to 906.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slide 45 ("Section 906")
Notes, Ch. 3 (SOX 906)
Sarbanes-Oxley Act §906, 18 U.S.C. §1350(c)

questions.prompt:
The SEC finds that the CEO of Marlowe Biotech signed certifications stating he had evaluated the company's disclosure controls and had disclosed all significant internal-control deficiencies to the auditors and audit committee. In fact, he never reviewed the controls and knew of two deficiencies he didn't disclose. Federal prosecutors are separately weighing criminal charges.

Which statement correctly matches the Sarbanes-Oxley sections to this conduct?

options.text: Section 302 is the criminal certification provision, and Section 906 governs the auditor's attestation on internal controls.
Section 404 requires the CEO's certification, and Section 806 sets the criminal penalties for false certifications.
Section 906 applies only to the CFO's statement, and Section 302 applies only to the CEO's statement.
Section 302 covers the false certification about controls (civil SEC action); Section 906 adds criminal penalties.

questions.explanation: Section 302 requires the CEO and CFO to certify each periodic report, including that they evaluated disclosure controls and disclosed significant deficiencies to the auditors and audit committee, and false certifications support SEC enforcement (Mintz's QSGI example). Section 906 is the separate criminal certification that the report complies and fairly presents. Section 404 covers management's internal-control report and the auditor's attestation, and 806 is whistleblower anti-retaliation. Both 302 and 906 apply to both the CEO and the CFO. This builds on your PA Q10 miss by pairing 302 with 906.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-6
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 44–46 (SOX 302, 906; QSGI case)
Notes, Ch. 3 (SOX 302, 906)
Sarbanes-Oxley Act §302 (15 U.S.C. §7241) and §906 (18 U.S.C. §1350)

questions.prompt:
The founders of Verdant Outfitters tell the board: "If we adopt conscious capitalism, we should stop worrying about profit entirely and put every dollar into social and environmental programs." A board member objects that this misreads the approach.

Which statement reflects conscious capitalism as Mintz describes it?

options.text: Profit still matters, but decisions serve a higher purpose and create value for all stakeholders.
The founders are right, because conscious capitalism replaces the profit motive with social and environmental goals.
Conscious capitalism means maximizing shareholder profit while staying within the rules of the game.
Conscious capitalism requires giving every employee stock options so they share in the profits.

questions.explanation: Mintz's first guiding principle says that while "profits are essential for a sustainable business, conscious capitalism focuses on purpose beyond profit," and decisions follow a stakeholder model that weighs effects on the whole ecosystem. Eliminating profit, the founders' view, was your answer on PA Q12, and it's the trap. Maximizing profit within the rules is Friedman's economic model (managerial capitalism). Stock options for everyone isn't part of the approach.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-5
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 38–40 (Conscious Capitalism; Economic Model of CSR)
Notes, Ch. 3 (Conscious Capitalism: purpose beyond profit)
Mackey & Sisodia, Conscious Capitalism (2013): four tenets
questions.hint: Purpose beyond profit isn't the same as no profit.

questions.prompt:
Tidewater Grocers has adopted conscious capitalism. In her first all-hands meeting, the new CEO commits to "embrace our purpose, create value for every stakeholder, and inspire the actions that build a conscious culture," and she starts doing so herself.

Which of the four guiding principles of conscious capitalism is the CEO personally modeling?

options.text: Higher purpose
Stakeholder orientation
Conscious culture
Conscious leadership

questions.explanation: Mintz defines conscious leadership as leaders who "embrace the company's purpose, create value for all stakeholders, and inspire actions that contribute to a conscious culture." Higher purpose is the company's reason for existing beyond profit. Stakeholder orientation is optimizing value for all stakeholders as a decision model. Conscious culture is the resulting climate of trust, care and cooperation. All four are real principles; the clue is that one person, the leader, is acting. This reinforces the conscious capitalism concept you missed on PA Q12.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-5
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slide 38 (Conscious Capitalism: 4 Guiding Principles)
Notes, Ch. 3 (Conscious Capitalism)
questions.hint: The quote describes what a person at the top does.

questions.prompt:
At Ridgeline Software, sales vice presidents pressure the accounting staff to book fourth-quarter deals early because the VPs' bonuses depend on quarterly revenue. The CEO wants to stop the pressure without scrapping a compensation plan that otherwise works well.

Which action best addresses the problem, according to Mintz?

options.text: Have top management set the tone, backing staff who refuse and making integrity outrank the target.
Eliminate all incentive pay across the company so that no one has any reason to manipulate the results.
Move the accounting department so that it reports to the audit committee instead of management.
Remove supervisors from the whistleblowing process so that all reports go straight to human resources.

questions.explanation: Mintz stresses that "support for ethical behavior from top management is a critical component of fostering an ethical climate," and that poor tone at the top discourages reporting and invites manipulation. Scrapping incentive pay was your answer on PA Q13. It treats a symptom, and the pressure can return in other forms if leadership doesn't model integrity. The audit committee oversees financial reporting but doesn't manage the accounting department. Rerouting all reports to HR doesn't change the culture driving the pressure.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 3 (begins p. 102), LO 3-3: "Ethics in the Workplace" section
Your Mintz Ch. 3 slides (2025 release): slides 13, 24 (poor tone at the top; Ethics in the Workplace)
Notes, Ch. 3 (fraud reporting discouraged by poor tone at top)
COSO, Internal Control—Integrated Framework (2013), Principle 1: commitment to integrity and ethical values
questions.hint: Fix the culture, not just the pay plan.

questions.prompt:
At Pellham Industries, the CEO tells managers, "Make the numbers, whatever it takes." Over the past year, two accountants who questioned aggressive estimates were transferred to remote offices, and other staff have stopped raising concerns.

Which two of Marianne Jennings' seven signs of ethical collapse do these facts show?

options.text: A weak board of directors, and conflicts of interest that are overlooked
Innovation like no other company, and goodness in some areas that atones for evil in others
Young 'uns with a bigger-than-life CEO, and a weak board of directors

questions.prompt:
An auditor plainly failed to follow GAAS when testing inventory. But the client sold the business at a price that wasn't affected by the inventory figures, and it can't identify any money it lost because of the faulty audit. It sues for professional negligence anyway.

Which element of a negligence claim is the client missing?

options.text: Duty
Damage
Breach of duty
Privity

questions.explanation: Professional negligence requires four elements. Duty: the accountant owed the plaintiff reasonable care. Breach: the accountant failed to use the skill normally possessed by public accountants. Damage: the plaintiff suffered damage. Causation: a causal nexus connects the breach and the damage. The auditor owed the client a duty and breached it by ignoring GAAS, but with no loss, there's no damage, so the claim fails. Privity isn't an element of negligence itself; it decides which third parties can sue.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 10 (Professional Negligence)
Notes, Ch. 8 (professional negligence must have duty, breach, damage, causation)
questions.hint: Can you sue for negligence when nothing was lost?

questions.prompt:
To meet a deadline, an audit manager skips the inventory observation. He knows that skipping it significantly raises the risk of missing a material misstatement. He doesn't intend to deceive anyone and hopes nothing is wrong.

Which liability theory best describes his conduct?

options.text: Ordinary negligence
Fraud
Negligent misrepresentation
Recklessness

questions.explanation: Mintz distinguishes these: negligence "occurs when a person unknowingly takes a risk that they should have been aware of," while "recklessness means to knowingly take a risk." Recklessness is short of intent to cause harm but greater than simple negligence. The manager knew the risk and chose it anyway, so this is recklessness. Fraud would also require a false representation made with scienter; the facts describe only his knowing acceptance of risk, which Mintz labels recklessness. Negligent misrepresentation involves giving false information to a known third party.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 13, 15 (Recklessness; Exhibit 8.3)
Notes, Ch. 8 (recklessness: knowingly taking a risk)
questions.hint: Did he know about the risk?

questions.prompt:
An auditor issues its report to Delmont Corp. Without the auditor's knowledge, a supplier the auditor had never heard of obtains a copy and relies on it to extend $2 million of credit. The supplier loses money and sues for negligent misrepresentation in a jurisdiction that follows the strict standard Mintz attributes to McCamish.

What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The supplier wins, because auditors are liable to all reasonably foreseeable users.
The supplier wins, because negligent misrepresentation requires no proof of reliance.
The supplier wins, as long as it proves the auditor acted with scienter.
The supplier likely loses, because it wasn't a known person relying for a known purpose.

questions.explanation: Mintz explains that "the ruling in McCamish applies a strict standard for determining who can assert a negligent misrepresentation claim": the plaintiff must be a "known person" who relies on the auditor's representations "for a known purpose." An unknown supplier fails that test. Liability to all reasonably foreseeable users is the broader Rosenblum approach, which most courts haven't followed. Reliance is a required element. Scienter is an element of fraud, not negligent misrepresentation.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-2: "Auditor Defenses to Negligence and Fraud" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 14, 32 (Negligent Misrepresentation; Auditor Defenses for Negligent Misrepresentation)
Notes, Ch. 8 (negligent misrepresentation; plaintiff must be a known person)
Restatement (Second) of Torts §552 (1977)
questions.hint: Known person, known purpose.

questions.prompt:
An investor who wasn't a client of the auditor sues for ordinary negligence in California after relying on audited financial statements she found online.

Under Bily v. Arthur Young, how is her claim likely to be treated?

options.text: California rejected foreseeability, so auditors generally aren't liable to non-clients for ordinary negligence.
California follows Rosenblum, so all reasonably foreseeable users may recover for ordinary negligence.
California requires only that she prove she read the audited statements before investing.
California bars every claim by non-clients, including claims for fraud.

questions.explanation: Mintz notes that Bily, a 1992 California Supreme Court case, "rejected [the] Rosenblum foreseeability approach," reasoning that foreseeability "exposes auditors to potential liability in excess of their proportionate share." Bily limits general negligence liability to the client, allows negligent misrepresentation claims by intended beneficiaries, and leaves fraud claims open to third parties. Rosenblum (New Jersey, 1983) is the foreseeability case Bily rejected. Reading the statements isn't enough to create a duty, and fraud claims remain available.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 19–20 (Reasonably Foreseeable Third Parties)
Bily v. Arthur Young & Co., 3 Cal. 4th 370 (1992)
H. Rosenblum, Inc. v. Adler, 93 N.J. 324 (1983)
questions.hint: Bily rejected one famous New Jersey case.

questions.prompt:
An insurer that wasn't the auditor's client sues the auditor for fraud, alleging the clean opinion was knowingly false. The auditor didn't specifically intend the insurer to rely on it. But the auditor knew the report would reach a class of investors like the insurer and that they would act on it.

Which standard from Mintz's Exhibit 8.6 supports the fraud claim?

options.text: "Should have known" from Blue Bell, which implies missing knowledge and applies in fraud cases
"Reason to expect" (Pacific Mutual), which reflects affirmative knowledge
"Near privity" from Credit Alliance, which applies only to fraud claims
"Reasonable foreseeability" from Rosenblum, which applies only to fraud claims

questions.explanation: Exhibit 8.6 contrasts the two. Blue Bell's "should have known" standard "implies a lack of knowledge that auditors should have possessed," and it doesn't support fraud. Pacific Mutual's "reason to expect" standard reflects "possession of affirmative knowledge," and it does. Pacific Mutual adopted the Restatement §531 "reason to expect" standard, which requires actual knowledge of an especial likelihood that the misrepresentation will reach and influence a particular person or class. That's knowledge the auditor has, not just foreseeability. (On its facts, the Texas Supreme Court ultimately ruled for Ernst & Young; Mintz's slide describes the standard, not the final result.) Credit Alliance's near privity and Rosenblum's foreseeability are negligence tests, not fraud tests.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-1: "Legal Liabilities of Auditors: An Overview" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 25–28 (Liability for Fraudulent Misrepresentation; Should Have Known; Reason to Expect; Exhibit 8.6)
Restatement (Second) of Torts §531 (1977)
Ernst & Young, L.L.P. v. Pacific Mutual Life Ins. Co., 51 S.W.3d 573 (Tex. 2001)
questions.hint: Fraud needs knowledge, not just what the auditor should have known.

questions.prompt:
Investors sue the auditor under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933. They argue only that the clean audit opinion in the registration statement "turned out to be wrong," because the company later restated its results.

After Omnicare, is that enough to state a claim?

options.text: Yes. Section 11 imposes strict liability whenever an opinion is objectively false.
No. Section 11 never applies to opinions, only to statements of fact.
Yes, as long as the investors also prove the auditor acted with scienter.
No. It's actionable only if not truly held, or it has a misleading embedded fact or omission.

questions.explanation: In Omnicare (2015), the Supreme Court held that an opinion "may not support Section 11 liability merely because it is ultimately found incorrect." Mintz applies that to auditors. An auditor is liable for its opinion only if it doesn't actually hold the opinion, if the opinion contains a misleading embedded fact, or if it omits facts that make it misleading. An omission claim must identify specific steps the auditor did or didn't take. Opinions can be actionable in those three situations, and Section 11 doesn't require scienter.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 40–43 (Section 11; Omnicare; Material Omission)
Notes, Ch. 8 (Section 11 liability)
Omnicare, Inc. v. Laborers District Council Construction Industry Pension Fund, 575 U.S. 175 (2015)
questions.hint: Being wrong isn't the same as being misleading.

questions.prompt:
An investor relied on a misleading statement in a 10-K filed with the SEC and sues the auditor under Section 18 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

What defense does Section 18 give the auditor?

options.text: Showing that, after a reasonable investigation, it had reason to believe the registration statement was true (the due diligence defense)
Showing it acted in good faith without knowing the statement was false or misleading
Showing that it had no contract with the investor
Showing that Section 18 applies only to registration statements for new offerings

questions.explanation: Section 18 imposes liability for material false or misleading statements in documents filed with the SEC. Mintz notes the auditor's liability "can be limited if the auditor can show that she 'acted in good faith and had no knowledge that such statement was false or misleading,'" and that courts have limited the defense when the auditor was grossly negligent. Due diligence is the Section 11 defense for registration statements under the 1933 Act. Privity isn't required, and Section 18 covers 1934 Act filings such as 10-Ks.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section

Notes, Ch. 8 (Section 18: good faith)
Securities Exchange Act §18(a), 15 U.S.C. §78r(a)

questions.prompt:
The SEC charges a mid-level accountant at a public company under Rule 13b2-1 for altering expense records to hide a budget overrun. He argues he can't be liable because he never intended to defraud anyone.

Is his defense likely to work?

options.text: Yes. Every federal securities violation requires intent to deceive.
Yes. Rule 13b2-1 applies only to the company, not to individual employees.
No, but only because the case also involves bribery of foreign officials.
No. Scienter isn't required, and a Rule 13b2-1 violation can rest on negligence.

questions.explanation: Mintz explains that Section 13(b)(2)(A) requires issuers to keep accurate books and records, that "scienter is not an element of the books-and-records and internal accounting controls provisions," and that Rule 13b2-1 "prohibits any person from directly or indirectly falsifying" books and records. A violation "may rest on a finding of negligence." The rule reaches any person, not just the company, and these provisions apply with or without bribery. They were enacted with the FCPA but aren't limited to bribery cases.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-3: "Statutory Liability" section

questions.prompt:
Plaintiffs in a securities fraud suit allege the auditor and executives had a motive to commit fraud: "keeping the stock price high." They offer no other facts about the defendants' state of mind.

Under the PSLRA's particularity standard, why is this allegation weak?

options.text: The PSLRA doesn't allow plaintiffs to allege any kind of motive in a securities fraud case.
Motive is irrelevant, because the PSLRA requires proof of negligence, not intent.
The allegation is enough, because any plausible motive establishes scienter.
Motive requires a concrete and personal benefit, not one shared by most insiders.

questions.explanation: Mintz explains that, under the PSLRA's particularity standard, courts have accepted scienter pled through particularized allegations of either strong circumstantial evidence of conscious misbehavior or recklessness, or motive and opportunity. Motive requires "a 'concrete and personal benefit' that would be realized from the fraud," and "keeping the stock prices high or other motives possessed by most corporate insiders are insufficient." In Tellabs, the Supreme Court required the inference of scienter to be at least as compelling as any opposing inference. Motive allegations are allowed, scienter is required, and a generic motive fails.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-4: "Private Securities Litigation Reform Act (PSLRA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 51–52 (PSLRA; Proportionate Liability)
Notes, Ch. 8 (PSLRA)
Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308 (2007); 15 U.S.C. §78u-4(b)(2)

questions.prompt:
In a securities class action, the plaintiffs' only evidence of the CEO's scienter is that he signed the company's Section 302 certifications. They offer no facts showing he knew about improper journal entries or weak controls.

Based on the cases Mintz discusses, what is the likely result?

options.text: Certifications alone don't create a strong inference of scienter without facts showing knowledge.
The certifications alone prove scienter, because the CEO swore the reports were accurate.
Section 302 certifications can never be considered as evidence of scienter.
Scienter isn't required, because Section 302 imposes strict liability on CEOs.

questions.explanation: Mintz contrasts two cases. In In re WatchGuard, "the individual defendants' 302 certifications were, by themselves, inadequate to support a strong inference of scienter." In In re Lattice Semiconductor, the certifications did support an inference because the plaintiffs alleged facts that the defendants knew about improper journal entries or inadequate controls. Higginbotham adds that scienter requires specific proof, not just an assertion. So certifications can count as evidence, but not on their own, and 302 doesn't create strict liability in private fraud suits.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-5: "SOX and Auditor Legal Liabilities" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slide 55 (SOX Section 302)
In re WatchGuard Securities Litigation (W.D. Wash. 2006); In re Lattice Semiconductor Corp. (D. Or. 2006); Higginbotham v. Baxter International, 495 F.3d 753 (7th Cir. 2007)
questions.hint: A signature plus what else?

questions.prompt:
A U.S. medical-device company is bidding on a hospital contract in another country. It pays reasonable airfare and hotel costs for three of that country's health ministry officials to visit its U.S. plant for a product demonstration. Nothing is paid beyond those costs.

Which FCPA affirmative defense best fits these facts?

options.text: The local law defense, since such visits are customary in the officials' country
The reasonable and bona fide expenditure defense
The facilitating payment exception for routine governmental action
The materiality defense, since the costs were small

questions.explanation: The FCPA has two affirmative defenses: (1) the payment was lawful under the foreign country's written laws, and (2) it was a reasonable and bona fide expenditure, such as travel and lodging, directly related to promoting, demonstrating, or explaining products or services, or to performing a contract. Paying for a product demonstration fits the second. The local law defense requires written law; custom or tolerance isn't enough. Facilitating payments speed up routine, non-discretionary actions, and awarding a contract is discretionary. The FCPA has no materiality defense.
sources: Mintz & Miller, 6th ed., Ch. 8 (begins p. 399), LO 8-6: "Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA)" section
Your Mintz Ch. 8 slides (2025 release): slides 57–58 (FCPA; Facilitating Payments vs. Bribes)
15 U.S.C. §§78dd-1(c), 78dd-2(c) (affirmative defenses) and §§78dd-1(b), 78dd-2(b) (routine governmental action)
DOJ & SEC, A Resource Guide to the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, 2nd ed. (2020)
questions.hint: Travel and lodging for a product demonstration.
